note: Dropped "For" that grounds the claim about the parts of my life.
replacement: 31. Nor would it help to suppose that I have always been as I am now: that would not let me escape these reasonings, because even then it would not follow that I need not look for an author of my existence. For the whole span of my life divides into infinitely many parts, and none of them depends on any other. So the fact that I existed a little while ago does not mean I must exist now, unless some cause creates me afresh at this moment, so to speak, that is, conserves me. Anyone who attentively considers the nature of duration will see perfectly clearly that a substance needs the same power and the same act to be conserved at each moment of its duration as it would need to be created if it did not yet exist. It is therefore manifestly a dictate of the natural light that conservation and creation differ only in our mode of thinking [and not in reality].

note: Dropped "for" linking the premise about unity to its reason.
replacement: 35. Nor can we suppose that several causes together produced me, so that I got the idea of one perfection I attribute to Deity from one cause and the idea of another from another, and that all those perfections are found somewhere in the universe but not all together in a single being, God. The reverse is the case: the unity, simplicity and inseparability of all the properties of Deity is itself one of the chief perfections I conceive him to have. The idea of this unity of all the perfections of Deity could certainly not have been put in my mind by a cause from which I had not also received the ideas of all the other perfections. For no power could make me grasp them in one inseparable unity without also giving me knowledge of what they were [and of their existence in a particular mode].

note: Dropped "for" that introduces the grounds of the inquiry.
replacement: 37. It remains only to ask how I received this idea from God, for I did not draw it from the senses, and it does not come upon me unexpectedly, as ideas of sensible objects usually do when these objects are presented, or seem to be presented, to the external sense organs. Nor is it merely something my mind made up or invented, since I cannot take anything away from it or add anything to it. The only alternative left, then, is that it is innate, as the idea of myself is.

note: Dropped "at least"; also "For" before the second sentence.
replacement: 39. Before I examine this more attentively and move on to other truths that can be drawn from it, I think it right to stay here for a while and contemplate God himself — to ponder his marvelous attributes at leisure, and to behold, admire and adore the beauty of this light so unspeakably great, as far, at least, as the strength of my mind, somewhat dazzled by the sight, will permit. For just as we learn by faith that the supreme felicity of the next life lies in contemplating the Divine majesty alone, so we learn from experience even now that a similar meditation, though incomparably less perfect, gives the highest satisfaction we are capable of in this life.

note: Dropped "for" before the premise about the maker.
replacement: 5. Still, this does not yet fully satisfy me. For error is not a pure negation, [in other words, not just the lack of some knowledge that is not owed to me]; it is a privation, the lack of some knowledge that it seems I ought to have. Yet when I think about the nature of God, it seems impossible that he would have planted in his creature a faculty not perfect of its kind, that is, one lacking a perfection that is due to it; for if it is true that the more skillful the maker, the more perfect his work, what could the supreme Creator of the universe have made that is not absolutely perfect in all its parts? And surely there is no doubt that God could have created me so that I would never be deceived; it is also certain that he always wills what is best. Is it better, then, for me to be capable of being deceived than not to be?

7. It also strikes me that, to judge the perfection of the works of Deity, we should not look at one creature in isolation but at all his creatures together. For something that might perhaps, with some show of reason, seem highly imperfect if it were alone in the world may still be the most perfect possible when seen as a part of the whole universe. It was my purpose to doubt everything, and so far I know with certainty only my own existence and God's. Nevertheless, having noted the infinite power of Deity, I cannot deny that he may have produced many other objects, or at least that he is able to produce them, so that I have a place as a part in relation to the great whole of his creatures.

note: Several proof "for" connectives dropped and "I experience" lost.
replacement: 8. Now I look at myself more closely and ask what my errors are (which alone show that there is imperfection in me). I observe that they depend on two causes working together: the faculty of cognition I have, and the faculty of election or power of free choice — in other words, the understanding and the will. For by the understanding alone I [neither affirm nor deny anything but] merely apprehend (percipio) the ideas about which I can form a judgment, and when it is taken precisely in this way, no error properly so called is found in it. There are perhaps countless objects in the world of which I have no idea in my understanding. Still, it cannot be said that I am deprived of those ideas [as of something due to my nature]; I simply do not have them. For there is really no ground for proving that Deity ought to have given me a larger faculty of cognition than he did. However skillful a workman I take him to be, I have no reason to think he was bound to give each of his works all the perfections he can give to some. Nor can I complain that God has not given me freedom of choice, or a will ample and perfect enough, since I am conscious of a will so wide and extended that it is superior to all limits. What strikes me as highly remarkable here is that among all my other properties there is none so great and perfect that I do not clearly discern it could be greater and more perfect still. Take the faculty of understanding: I find it very small in extent and greatly limited, and yet I form the idea of another faculty of the same nature, much more ample and even infinite; and since I can frame the idea of it, I discover from that fact alone that it belongs to the nature of God. Likewise, if I examine memory or imagination or any other faculty I have, I find each one small and circumscribed, and in God immense [and infinite]. It is only the faculty of will, or freedom of choice, that I experience to be so great that I cannot conceive the idea of one more ample and extended. So it is chiefly my will that makes me discern that I bear a certain image and similitude of Deity. For although the faculty of will is incomparably greater in God than in me, both because of the knowledge and power joined with it, which make it stronger and more efficacious, and because of its object, since in him it extends to more things, it nevertheless does not appear to me greater, considered in itself formally and precisely. For the power of will consists only in this: that we are able to do or not to do the same thing (that is, to affirm or deny, to pursue or shun it); or, better, in this alone: that when we affirm or deny, pursue or shun, what the understanding proposes to us, we act without being conscious of any external force determining us to a particular action. For freedom does not require me to be equally indifferent toward each of two contraries. On the contrary, the more I incline toward one of them, whether because I clearly know that the reason of truth and goodness is in it or because God so disposes my thought from within, the more freely I choose and embrace it. Divine grace and natural knowledge, far from reducing liberty, assuredly increase and strengthen it. The indifference I am conscious of when no reason impels me to one side rather than the other is the lowest grade of liberty: it shows a defect or negation of knowledge rather than a perfection of will. For if I always clearly knew what was true and good, I would never have trouble deciding what judgment to form or what choice to make, and so I would be entirely free without ever being indifferent.

note: Dropped "because" giving the reason for not complaining.
replacement: 15. And finally, I should not complain that God concurs with me in forming the acts of this will, the judgments in which I am deceived, because, in so far as they depend on God, those acts are wholly true and good, and being able to form them is a higher degree of perfection in my nature than being unable would be. Privation, in which alone the formal reason of error and sin consists, needs no concurrence of Deity, because it is not a thing [or existence]; and if it is referred to God as its cause, it should be called not privation but negation [in the sense these words have in the schools]. For in truth it is no imperfection in Deity that he has given me the power to give or withhold my assent on certain matters of which he has not put a clear and distinct knowledge in my understanding. But it is doubtless an imperfection in me that I do not use my freedom rightly, and readily pass judgment on matters I conceive only obscurely and confusedly. I perceive, nevertheless, that Deity could easily have made me so that I would never be deceived while still remaining free and having limited knowledge. He could have done this by implanting in my understanding a clear and distinct knowledge of everything I would ever have to deliberate about; or simply by engraving so deeply on my memory the resolution never to judge anything without first conceiving it clearly and distinctly that I could never forget it. And I easily understand that, considering myself as a single whole, with no reference to any other being in the universe, I would have been much more perfect than I am if Deity had created me superior to error. But I cannot therefore deny that it is somehow a greater perfection in the universe for some of its parts not to be exempt from defect, as others are, than for all of them to be perfectly alike. And I have no right to complain that God, who placed me in the world, did not want me to hold that rank which is the chief and most perfect of all.

16. I even have good reason to be content. He has not given me the perfection of being superior to error by the first means I noted above, which depends on clear and evident knowledge of everything I can deliberate about. But he has at least left in my power the other means: to hold firmly to the resolution never to judge where the truth is not clearly known to me. For, although I am conscious of the weakness that I cannot keep my mind continually fixed on the same thought, I can nevertheless, by attentive and oft-repeated meditation, impress that resolution so strongly on my memory that I will never fail to recall it when I need it, and in this way I can acquire the habit of not erring.
